youtube.title: WebRTC-Direct: gRPC Peers With No Signaling Server | grpc-over-datachannels
youtube.description:
WebRTC-Direct examples for grpc-over-datachannels: a server listens on UDP and prints one certhash multiaddr; a client dials that address and gets an RTCDataChannel carrying generated gRPC. Direct on a LAN, relayed through TURN behind symmetric NAT, or full ICE with STUN in peer mode — generated examples in every supported language.

Code: https://github.com/browser-grpc/grpc-over-datachannels
Direct examples: https://github.com/browser-grpc/grpc-over-datachannels/tree/master/examples/direct
Blog: https://c100k.blogspot.com/2026/10/webrtc-direct-examples-in-every.html

Built with Fish Audio

scenes.heading: WebRTC Without Signaling
scenes.sub: One address printed. One dial. A data channel.
scenes.say: WebRTC usually starts with a signaling server, just so two peers can introduce themselves. This is WebRTC-Direct: a server prints one address, a client dials it, and a data channel opens. No introductions.

scenes.heading: The usual ceremony
bullets: Peers exchange SDP through a signaling service you must run
Signaling is one more moving part to deploy and secure
Most examples stop at the browser demo stage
scenes.say: The standard ceremony needs a signaling service, an offer and answer exchange, and only then a connection. That service is one more moving part to deploy, secure, and keep running, and most examples never get past it.

scenes.heading: Dial the multiaddr
bullets: Server binds UDP and prints a certhash multiaddr
The certificate hash is the identity; the address is the intro
A Direct listener needs no STUN server at all
scenes.say: A Direct server binds a U D P socket and prints a multiaddr whose certhash names its D T L S certificate. The client dials that address and verifies the hash as it connects. Identity and introduction in one string, and no S T U N server involved.

scenes.heading: Three ways through
bullets: Direct: plain UDP on a LAN or a reachable host
TURN: relayed through an allocation for symmetric NAT
Peer mode: full ICE with STUN, SDP exchanged out of band
scenes.say: There are three ways through. Direct is plain U D P, on a local network or any reachable host. For symmetric N A T, the same server is reached through a T U R N relay; the server never changes. And where you want full I C E, peer mode gathers candidates with S T U N and exchanges S D P out of band, through files in the examples.

scenes.heading: Every generated language
bullets: Embedded stacks dial and serve natively in Go and Rust
Sidecar examples for the other languages use the same address
The gRPC code on top is identical either way
scenes.say: The embedded stacks serve and dial natively. The other languages use generated sidecar examples that reach the same listener at the same address. The g R P C code above the channel does not change; only the way the channel is opened does.

scenes.heading: Honest limits
bullets: Browsers cannot dial multiaddrs: no raw UDP in the browser
Direct needs a reachable UDP path between the peers
A TCP-only tunnel cannot carry the TURN leg
scenes.say: The limits, honestly. Browsers cannot dial multiaddrs, because browsers do not get raw U D P. Direct needs a reachable U D P path, or a relay. And a T C P-only tunnel cannot carry the data channel's U D P legs, so browser plus tunnel plus T U R N is not a supported shape. The examples say exactly this, in writing.

scenes.heading: Live: dial the printed address
scenes.say: Here it is live. The server prints its multiaddr; the client dials it directly and the echo comes back over the data channel. Every other language does the same thing, natively or through the generated sidecar transport.

scenes.heading: Run the examples
bullets: Compose profiles: host, turn, stun, sidecar
scenes.say: The examples ship with compose profiles for the host, relay, S T U N, and sidecar shapes, and run in the project's C I containers. If you need g R P C between two machines without standing up an introducer, start there. Links are in the description.
